summary: Training volume over the past 4 weeks has been critically low — only 4 sessions totalling roughly 158 minutes of structured work — while sleep has been chronically insufficient, averaging under 6 hours most nights and body battery frequently bottoming out below 20. The swim base is the most underdeveloped discipline relative to the Half Oceanman (5,000m) in 28 days, with the longest open-water effort to date being just 2km at a high HR of 160bpm. Immediate priorities must be maximising swim-specific volume and quality in the remaining weeks while continuing to protect recovery given the persistently depleted wellness markers.
suggestions: Make pool swimming your primary focus for the next 4 weeks: aim for 3 sessions per week targeting progressive continuous blocks — the Half Oceanman 5,000m swim is 28 days away and your longest swim to date is only 2km at near-maximal HR, so sustained aerobic swim endurance is the biggest gap to close.

Address sleep as a performance variable — consistently sleeping under 5–6 hours is suppressing adaptation and keeping body battery chronically low; aim for a minimum 7-hour sleep window nightly, especially in the 10 days before the Half Oceanman.

Reduce the Saturday long ride (Sep 12) from 110km to a more controlled 70–80km at pure Z2 (128–145W), since your current cycling base from the last 4 weeks is a single 46-min indoor ride and jumping to a 4-hour effort risks excessive fatigue ahead of race day.

For the Sep 13 long run, cap at 14–16km easy rather than 20km — your running base shows no recorded runs in the last 4 weeks, so a 20km long run this early risks injury or deep fatigue that compromises swim quality in the final pre-race week.

In the final 7 days before the Half Oceanman (from Sep 26 onward), shift fully into taper mode: swim one short confidence session of 2,000m easy, eliminate all intensity, keep the body fresh — arriving rested matters far more than adding last-minute volume.
